title: What If Students Get Too Personal?
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Responding to a reader's dilemma about a student-teacher relationship becoming too personal, Dave Stuart Jr. addresses how to stay warm and caring without letting the job of "teacher" absorb too much of the jobs of "counselor" or "parent." He acknowledges there's no hard-and-fast rule, but after eighteen years he's developed a felt sense for when a relationship is drifting too personal, and he offers four concrete boundary-setting moves: steering MGC questions toward students' interests and aspirations rather than home life or relationship drama; redirecting heavy disclosures with a simple "Do you have anyone you can talk to about this?"; immediately looping in counselors, admin, or social workers when a student shares something serious like thoughts of self-harm; and keeping his classroom closed except by appointment during lunch and after school to protect his own time. He frames these as gentle but firm signals of a professional line rather than coldness, aimed at protecting both his capacity to teach well and his own boundaries against bringing work home.
points: Stuart's core boundary-setting principle is steering MGC questions toward students' own interests and aspirations rather than home life or relationship drama, preventing overly personal disclosures before they start.
For students who do bring up heavy topics, his go-to redirect — "Do you have anyone you can talk to about this?" — signals connector rather than confidant without shutting the student down.
He draws a hard line at safety-relevant disclosures (self-harm, intense depression, unsafe home), routing those immediately to counselors, admin, or social workers rather than handling them himself.
Keeping his classroom closed except by appointment during lunch and after school is framed explicitly as boundary-protection against bringing work home, not as a rejection of students.
He credits eighteen years of experience with developing a felt "sense" for when a relationship is drifting too personal, acknowledging there's no formula, only accumulated judgment.
quotes: We want our students to know that we care — and to help with that, we need to actually care — but then again, our sanity and time constraints require us to keep the job of "teacher" from taking on too much of the jobs of "counselor" or "parent.
I've noticed a growing "sense" for when a student-teacher relationship is becoming too personal.
If a student does bring up these kinds of extra-personal, thorny topics, I like to ask things like, "Do you have anyone you can talk to about this?

If a student ever shares something super heavy (e.g., thoughts of self-harm, intense depression or anxiety, unsafe home), I get the student connected with the proper folks ASAP (e.g., counselor, admin, social worker, etc.).
It's a gentle but firm assertion of a boundary that I need in order to not bring work home, which is very important to me.
